question: How does uv cache Git dependencies?
answer: According to the context, uv caches Git dependencies based on the fully-resolved Git commit hash. When you run `uv pip compile`, it will pin Git dependencies to a specific commit hash when writing the resolved dependency set. Additionally, if a Git dependency references a branch (like main), uv will prefer the locked commit SHA in an existing `uv.lock` file over the latest commit on that branch, unless the `--upgrade` or `--upgrade-package` flags are used.

contexts.text:
Introduction
  





    Concepts
  





Caching
Dependency caching
uv uses aggressive caching to avoid re-downloading (and re-building) dependencies that have already
been accessed in prior runs.
The specifics of uv's caching semantics vary based on the nature of the dependency:

For registry dependencies (like those downloaded from PyPI), uv respects HTTP caching headers.
For direct URL dependencies, uv respects HTTP caching headers, and also caches based on the
  URL itself.
For Git dependencies, uv caches based on the fully-resolved Git commit hash. As such,
  uv pip compile will pin Git dependencies to a specific commit hash when writing the resolved
  dependency set.

Caching
Persisting the uv cache between workflow runs can improve performance.
uv-install:
  variables:
    UV_CACHE_DIR: .uv-cache
  cache:
    - key:
        files:
          - uv.lock
      paths:
        - $UV_CACHE_DIR
  script:
    # Your `uv` commands
  after_script:
    - uv cache prune --ci

See the GitLab caching documentation for more details on
configuring caching.
Using uv cache prune --ci at the end of the job is recommended to reduce cache size. See the uv
cache documentation for more details.
Using uv pip
If using the uv pip interface instead of the uv project interface, uv requires a virtual
environment by default. To allow installing packages into the system environment, use the --system
flag on all uv invocations or set the UV_SYSTEM_PYTHON variable.

uv blocks cache-modifying operations while other uv commands are running. By default, those
uv cache commands have a 5 min timeout waiting for other uv processes to terminate to avoid
deadlocks. This timeout can be changed with
UV_LOCK_TIMEOUT. In cases where it is known that no
other uv processes are reading or writing from the cache, --force can be used to ignore the lock.
Caching in continuous integration
It's common to cache package installation artifacts in continuous integration environments (like
GitHub Actions or GitLab CI) to speed up subsequent runs.
By default, uv caches both the wheels that it builds from source and the pre-built wheels that it
downloads directly, to enable high-performance package installation.

For local dependencies, uv caches based on the last-modified time of the source archive (i.e.,
  the local .whl or .tar.gz file). For directories, uv caches based on the last-modified time of
  the pyproject.toml, setup.py, or setup.cfg file.
For flat indexes (i.e., --find-links locations), uv assumes the index contents are
  immutable, caching each file by name. As such, replacing a file with new contents under the same
  name (e.g., rebuilding a wheel into a --find-links directory) will not be picked up until the
  cache is refreshed.

If you're running into caching issues, uv includes a few escape hatches:

To clear the cache entirely, run uv cache clean. To clear the cache for a specific package, run
  uv cache clean <package-name>.

Note
uv applies similar logic to Git dependencies. For example, if a Git dependency references
the main branch, uv will prefer the locked commit SHA in an existing uv.lock file over
the latest commit on the main branch, unless the --upgrade or --upgrade-package flags
are used.

These flags can also be provided to uv sync or uv run to update the lockfile and the
environment.
Exporting the lockfile
If you need to integrate uv with other tools or workflows, you can export uv.lock to different
formats including requirements.txt, pylock.toml (PEP 751), and CycloneDX SBOM.
$ uv export --format requirements.txt
$ uv export --format pylock.toml
$ uv export --format cyclonedx1.5

See the export guide for comprehensive documentation on all export formats and their
use cases.

question: My project uses setuptools-scm, and uv doesn't rebuild it when the commit changes. How do I fix that?
answer:
To fix this, add cache key entries to your `pyproject.toml` that include both the `pyproject.toml` file and Git commit information:

```toml
[tool.uv]
cache-keys = [{ file = "pyproject.toml" }, { git = { commit = true } }]
```

This tells uv to rebuild your package whenever either the `pyproject.toml` file changes or the Git commit hash changes. If your dynamic metadata also depends on Git tags, you can expand it to:

```toml
[tool.uv]
cache-keys = [{ file = "pyproject.toml" }, { git = { commit = true, tags = true } }]
```

By default, uv will only rebuild and reinstall local directory dependencies (e.g., editables) if
the pyproject.toml, setup.py, or setup.cfg file in the directory root has changed, or if a
src directory is added or removed. This is a heuristic and, in some cases, may lead to fewer

When publishing a package, we recommend running uv build --no-sources to ensure that the package
builds correctly when tool.uv.sources is disabled, as is the case when using other build tools,
like pypa/build.

A regular installation of a directory with a Python package first builds a wheel and then installs
that wheel into your virtual environment, copying all source files.

be rebuilt whenever the commit hash or dependencies change, you can add the following to the
project's pyproject.toml:
pyproject.toml[tool.uv]
cache-keys = [{ file = "pyproject.toml" }, { git = { commit = true } }]

key to include the tags:

tool.uv.reinstall-package list:
pyproject.toml[tool.uv]

It's safe to run multiple uv commands concurrently, even against the same virtual environment. uv's
cache is designed to be thread-safe and append-only, and thus robust to multiple concurrent readers

question: What is the difference between running a tool with uvx and installing it with uv tool install?
answer:
# Difference Between uvx and uv tool install

**uvx (uv tool run):**
- Runs tools without installation in a temporary, isolated virtual environment
- The environment is cached in the uv cache directory but treated as disposable
- Running `uv cache clean` will delete the environment
- Best for one-off tool executions

**uv tool install:**
- Permanently installs the tool in a persistent tools/ subdirectory
- Creates an isolated virtual environment that persists after the command completes
- Tool executables are added to PATH and available system-wide
- Useful when other programs need access to the tool or in Docker images

treated as disposable, i.e., if you run uv cache clean the environment will be deleted. The
environment is only cached to reduce the overhead of repeated invocations. If the environment is
removed, a new one will be created automatically.

installation using uv tool run, in which case their dependencies are installed in a temporary
virtual environment isolated from the current project.
Because it is very common to run tools without installing them, a uvx alias is provided for

dependencies.

However, sometimes the package and command names differ.

--with-executables-from flag.

Use the UV_TOOL_BIN_DIR environment variable to configure the tool executable directory.

are installed into the executable directory.

question: How do I make uv always install torch from the PyTorch CPU index instead of PyPI?
answer:
To make uv always install torch from the PyTorch CPU index, add the following to your `pyproject.toml`:

```toml
[[tool.uv.index]]
name = "pytorch"
url = "https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu"
explicit = true

[tool.uv.sources]
torch = { index = "pytorch" }
```

The `explicit = true` setting ensures the index is only used for PyTorch packages, while other dependencies continue to come from PyPI. This configuration guarantees torch is installed from the CPU-only PyTorch index rather than the default PyPI.

contexts.text:

$ # With an environment variable.
$ UV_TORCH_BACKEND=auto uv pip install torch

existing index configuration for any packages outside the PyTorch ecosystem.

UV_TORCH_BACKEND=cu130):

question: In a uv workspace with an app at the root and libraries under packages/, how many lockfiles are there, and how do I run a command for one library?
answer:
In a uv workspace, there is **one lockfile** shared across all packages, ensuring consistent dependencies across the entire workspace.

To run a command for a specific library, use the `--package` argument with `uv run` or `uv sync`. For example:

```
uv run --package library-name pytest
```

This allows you to execute commands in a particular workspace member from any workspace directory, while maintaining the single shared lockfile.

contexts.text:
Unlike requirements.txt files, the uv.lock file can represent arbitrary groups of dependencies,
so multiple files are not needed to lock development dependencies.
The uv lockfile is always universal, so
multiple files are not needed to
lock dependencies for each platform. This ensures that all
developers are using consistent, locked versions of dependencies regardless of their machine.
The uv lockfile also supports concepts like
pinning packages to specific indexes,
which is not representable in requirements.txt files.

Tip
If you only need to lock for a subset of platforms, use the
tool.uv.environments setting
to limit the resolution and lockfile.

To learn more, see the lockfile documentation.

Think: a FastAPI-based web application, alongside a series of libraries that are
versioned and maintained as separate Python packages, all in the same Git repository.
In a workspace, each package defines its own pyproject.toml, but the workspace shares a single
lockfile, ensuring that the workspace operates with a consistent set of dependencies.
As such, uv lock operates on the entire workspace at once, while uv run and uv sync operate on
the workspace root by default, though both accept a --package argument, allowing you to run a
command in a particular workspace member from any workspace directory.
Getting started
To create a workspace, add a tool.uv.workspace table to a pyproject.toml, which will implicitly
create a workspace rooted at that package.

RUN --mount=from=uv,source=/uv,target=/bin/uv \
    --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/uv \
    --mount=type=bind,source=uv.lock,target=uv.lock \
    --mount=type=bind,source=pyproject.toml,target=pyproject.toml \
    uv export --frozen --no-emit-workspace --no-dev --no-editable -o requirements.txt && \
    uv pip install -r requirements.txt --target "${LAMBDA_TASK_ROOT}"

# If you have a workspace, copy it over and install it too.
#
# By omitting `--no-emit-workspace`, `library` will be copied into the task root. Using a separate
# `RUN` command ensures that all third-party dependencies are cached separately and remain
# robust to changes in the workspace.

The preferred way to execute commands in the environment is with uv run, e.g.:
$ uv run pytest

Prior to every uv run invocation, uv will verify that the lockfile is up-to-date with the
pyproject.toml, and that the environment is up-to-date with the lockfile, keeping your project

question: I run uvx ruff and later a new Ruff release comes out. Will uvx use it, and how do I force the newest version?
answer:
No, `uvx ruff` will not automatically use the new version. It will use the cached version unless the cache is refreshed.

To force the newest version, use the `@latest` suffix:

```
$ uvx ruff@latest --version
```

Alternatively, you can use the `--isolated` flag to ignore the cached version:

```
$ uvx --isolated ruff --version
```

question: What does pnpm's minimumReleaseAge setting do, and what unit is it in?
answer:
According to the context, `minimumReleaseAge` defines the minimum number of **minutes** that must pass after a version is published before pnpm will install it. This applies to all dependencies, including transitive ones.

For example, setting `minimumReleaseAge: 1440` ensures that only packages released at least one day ago can be installed. The built-in default is 1440 minutes (one day), which is non-strict for backward compatibility.

question: How do I approve one dependency's build script and deny another's with pnpm?
answer:
You can approve and deny build scripts using the `pnpm approve-builds` command with package names as arguments. Prefix a package name with `!` to deny it:

```
pnpm approve-builds esbuild !core-js
```

This approves `esbuild` to run its build scripts and denies `core-js`. The approved dependencies are added to the `allowBuilds` map in `pnpm-workspace.yaml` with a value of `true`, while denied ones are saved with a value of `false`.

Alternatively, you can use the `--allow-build` flag during install:
```
pnpm install --allow-build=esbuild --allow-build='!core-js'
```

question: What is pnpr?
answer:
pnpr is a pnpm-compatible registry server written in Rust that speaks the npm registry protocol. It allows npm-compatible clients (pnpm, npm, yarn) to communicate with it. pnpr hosts your own packages and proxies upstream registries like registry.npmjs.org, with its own authentication and access controls—similar to verdaccio's role in the JavaScript ecosystem.

Since v0.1.0-alpha.11, pnpr can serve multiple package types, supporting the Cargo and Python protocols as well as the OCI distribution API. This allows workspaces to publish packages, crates, Python distributions, and images in a single transaction. Users can sign in through OpenID Connect.

pnpm add pypi:httpx

pnpm add pypi:httpx@0.28.1

question: In pnpm filtering, what is the difference between --filter foo... and --filter ...foo?
answer:
Based on the context:

- **`--filter foo...`** selects a package and its dependencies (direct and non-direct). It runs commands for foo and all packages that foo depends on.

- **`--filter ...foo`** selects a package and its dependents (direct and non-direct). It runs commands for foo and all packages that depend on foo.

In short: `foo...` goes downstream to dependencies, while `...foo` goes upstream to dependents.

FilteringFiltering allows you to restrict commands to specific subsets of packages.
pnpm supports a rich selector syntax for picking packages by name or by
relation.
Selectors may be specified via the --filter (or -F) flag:
pnpm --filter <package_selector> <command>

Matching#
--filter <package_name>#
To select an exact package, just specify its name (@scope/pkg) or use a
pattern to select a set of packages (@scope/*).
Examples:
pnpm --filter "@babel/core" test
pnpm --filter "@babel/*" test
pnpm --filter "*core" test

Specifying the scope of the package is optional, so --filter=core will pick @babel/core if core is not found.

pnpm --filter "./packages/**" <cmd>

Includes all projects that are under the specified directory.
It may be used with the ellipsis and chevron operators to select
dependents/dependencies as well:
pnpm --filter ...{<directory>} <cmd>
pnpm --filter {<directory>}... <cmd>
pnpm --filter ...{<directory>}... <cmd>

It may also be combined with [<since>]. For instance, to select all changed
projects inside a directory:
pnpm --filter "{packages/**}[origin/master]" <cmd>
pnpm --filter "...{packages/**}[origin/master]" <cmd>
pnpm --filter "{packages/**}[origin/master]..." <cmd>
pnpm --filter "...{packages/**}[origin/master]..." <cmd>

The pattern language is the usual one: * and ?

When
the first selector is an exclusion, filtering starts from every project in the
workspace. You can use as many filters as you want:
pnpm --filter ...foo --filter bar --filter baz... test

--filter-prod <filtering_pattern>#
Acts the same as --filter but omits devDependencies when selecting dependency projects
from the workspace.
--test-pattern <glob>#
test-pattern allows detecting whether the modified files are related to tests.
If they are, the dependent packages of such modified packages are not included.
This option is useful with the "changed since" filter.

For instance, this will run a command in all projects except for foo:
pnpm --filter=!foo <cmd>

And this will run a command in all projects that are not under the lib
directory:

inclusion can bring back a project that an earlier exclusion removed:

When packages are filtered, every package is taken that matches at least one of

the first selector is an exclusion, filtering starts from every project in the
workspace.

instance, the next command will run tests for all of foo's
dependencies:

question: Several AI coding agents work on the same pnpm monorepo in separate git worktrees. How do I avoid recreating node_modules hardlinks in every checkout, and what is the setting called now?
answer:
To avoid recreating node_modules hardlinks in every checkout, use pnpm's **global virtual store** by setting `virtualStoreType: global` in your configuration.

With this setting enabled, each worktree's node_modules contains only symlinks pointing to a single content-addressable store on disk, rather than duplicating hardlinks. This means:

- Subsequent installs in other worktrees are nearly instant—they only create symlinks
- Adding a new agent is fast and costs almost no extra disk space
- Dependencies are shared across all worktrees through one shared store

You can find the global store location by running `pnpm store path`. This approach is practical for multi-agent development since each agent gets an isolated working directory while sharing the underlying package contents.

question: List three pnpm settings that reduce supply-chain risk and what each one does.
answer:

question: How do I configure the module-name for namespace packages in uv, and what is the correct project structure I need to set up when packaging a module called bar in a shared namespace foo?

# Configuring Namespace Packages in uv

For a module `bar` in a shared namespace `foo`, use a **dotted module-name** in your configuration.

**Project Structure:**
```
pyproject.toml
src
└── foo
    └── bar
        └── __init__.py
```

**Configuration in pyproject.toml:**
```toml
[tool.uv.build-backend]
module-name = "foo.bar"
```

The dot in the module-name identifies it as a namespace package. This is the recommended approach for namespace packages with a single root `__init__.py`. 

Alternatively, if you have multiple root modules under the same namespace, you can use `namespace = true`, but this disables safety checks and is only recommended for legacy projects.

question: How does uv handle SIGINT signals when managing child processes in Unix environments?
answer: On Unix systems, uv forwards SIGINT to the child process only if it is sent more than once or if the child process group differs from uv's. This is because terminals send SIGINT to the foreground process group on Ctrl-C, so uv avoids forwarding a single SIGINT to prevent interfering with the child process's normal signal handling. Additionally, uv forwards most other signals (except SIGKILL, SIGCHLD, SIGIO, and SIGPOLL) to the child process to maintain proper process control.

# Relationship Between `pyproject.toml` and `uv.lock`

**`pyproject.toml`** specifies broad dependency requirements for your project, while **`uv.lock`** contains exact resolved versions of those dependencies.

The `pyproject.toml` defines what your project needs (e.g., "fastapi", "pydantic>2"), whereas `uv.lock` captures the precise versions that will be installed across all platforms and Python versions.

**For reproducibility:** The `uv.lock` file should be checked into version control, ensuring consistent and reproducible installations across different machines and developers. This guarantees that everyone working on the project uses the same package versions.

In summary: `pyproject.toml` = flexible requirements; `uv.lock` = exact, reproducible environment specifications.

# UV Credentials and Authentication

**Credential Handling:**
- UV does not persist Git credentials to `pyproject.toml` or `uv.lock` files for security reasons, as these are often included in source control
- Credentials may be automatically persisted if a Git credential helper is configured
- Only HTTPS Basic authentication is currently supported for packaging operations
- Credentials are not validated, so incorrect credentials won't immediately fail

**Current Limitation:**
The main limitation is that **credentials will not yet be used for Git requests**. They are only used for packaging operations that require fetching content from services.

**Authentication Methods:**
- SSH authentication using `ssh://` protocol
- HTTP authentication with personal access tokens
- Git credential helpers (recommended approach)

**Credential Management:**
Users can log out using `uv auth logout` or view stored credentials with `uv auth token`.

# Running pytest with uv

**Use `uv run pytest`** for testing in your project.

## Key Difference

- **`uv run`**: Runs tools within your project environment, with access to your project's dependencies. Use this for pytest and mypy.

- **`uv tool run` (or `uvx`)**: Runs tools in isolated, temporary environments without access to your project. Not suitable for testing.

## Why the Distinction Matters

If you use `uv tool run pytest`, the tool runs isolated from your project, so it won't have access to your project's installed dependencies. Since pytest needs to import and test your project code, you must use `uv run pytest` instead.

Before each invocation, `uv run` verifies the lockfile is up-to-date and the environment is synchronized, ensuring consistent, locked execution.

# Configuring uv-managed Projects with Jupyter in VS Code

**Setup Steps:**
1. Create a project: `uv init project`
2. Navigate to the directory: `cd project`
3. Add ipykernel as a dev dependency: `uv add --dev ipykernel`
4. Open in VS Code: `code .`
5. Create a new Jupyter notebook via the command palette
6. Select the project's virtual environment as the kernel

**Key Requirements:**
- ipykernel must be present in the project environment (either as a dev dependency or installed via `uv pip install ipykernel`)

**Important Considerations:**
- Packages installed via `%pip install` within notebooks modify the virtual environment but won't update `pyproject.toml` or `uv.lock` files
- Dependencies installed this way persist only for the current session
- For reliable dependency management, add packages to `pyproject.toml` instead

Using uv with Jupyter
The Jupyter notebook is a popular tool for interactive computing, data
analysis, and visualization. You can use Jupyter with uv in a few different ways, either to interact
with a project, or as a standalone tool.
Using Jupyter within a project
If you're working within a project, you can start a Jupyter
server with access to the project's virtual environment via the following:
$ uv run --with jupyter jupyter lab

By default, jupyter lab will start the server at
http://localhost:8888/lab.

For example, given:
$ uv venv --seed
$ uv run --with jupyter jupyter lab

Subsequent %pip install invocations within the notebook will install packages into the project's
virtual environment. However, such modifications will not be reflected in the project's
pyproject.toml or uv.lock files.
Using Jupyter as a standalone tool
If you ever need ad hoc access to a notebook (i.e., to run a Python snippet interactively), you can
start a Jupyter server at any time with uv tool run jupyter lab. This will run a Jupyter server in
an isolated environment.
Using Jupyter with a non-project environment
If you need to run Jupyter in a virtual environment that isn't associated with a
project (e.g., has no pyproject.toml or uv.lock), you can do
so by adding Jupyter to the environment directly.

$ cd project

# Add ipykernel as a dev dependency.
$ uv add --dev ipykernel

# Open the project in VS Code.
$ code .

Once the project directory is open in VS Code, you can create a new Jupyter notebook by selecting
"Create: New Jupyter Notebook" from the command palette. When prompted to select a kernel, choose
"Python Environments" and select the virtual environment you created earlier (e.g.,
.venv/bin/python on macOS and Linux, or .venv\Scripts\python on Windows).

Note
VS Code requires ipykernel to be present in the project environment. If you'd prefer to avoid
adding ipykernel as a dev dependency, you can install it directly into the project environment
with uv pip install ipykernel.

question: How do I enable preview features in uv.toml for my Python project?
answer:
To enable preview features in `uv.toml`, add the following configuration:

```
preview-features = ["foo", "bar"]
```

Replace `"foo"` and `"bar"` with the specific preview features you want to enable.

Alternatively, you can enable all preview features at once:

```
preview-features = true
```

You can also enable preview features in the `[tool.uv]` section of `pyproject.toml` or PEP 723 metadata using the same syntax.

Some preview features take effect before configuration files are loaded and cannot be enabled from

For backwards compatibility, enabling preview features that do not exist will warn, but not error,

Often, preview features can be used without changing any preview settings if the behavior change is

question: How do I use artifacts-keyring to authenticate with Azure Artifacts in uv?
answer:
To use artifacts-keyring to authenticate with Azure Artifacts in uv:

1. **Pre-install required packages** from a source other than Artifacts (since they're needed for authentication):
   - keyring package
   - artifacts-keyring plugin

2. **Enable keyring subprocess mode**:
   ```
   export UV_KEYRING_PROVIDER=subprocess
   ```

3. **Configure your index** in `pyproject.toml`:
   ```
   [[tool.uv.index]]
   name = "private-registry"
   url = "https://pkgs.dev.azure.com/<ORGANIZATION>/<PROJECT>/_packaging/<FEED>/pypi/simple/"
   ```

The artifacts-keyring plugin wraps the Azure Artifacts Credential Provider tool, which supports multiple authentication modes including interactive login. The keyring executable must be in your PATH (installed globally or in your active environment).

To configure the publish-url for a FEED in Azure Artifacts, add it to your `pyproject.toml` file under `[tool.uv.index]`:

```toml
[[tool.uv.index]]
name = "private-registry"
url = "https://pkgs.dev.azure.com/<ORGANIZATION>/<PROJECT>/_packaging/<FEED>/pypi/simple/"
publish-url = "https://pkgs.dev.azure.com/<ORGANIZATION>/<PROJECT>/_packaging/<FEED>/pypi/upload/"
```

Replace `<ORGANIZATION>`, `<PROJECT>`, and `<FEED>` with your actual values. Then configure credentials and publish using `uv publish --index private-registry`.

question: How does uv handle caching for local dependencies that is defined in setup.cfg file, and what options do I have if caching is causing problems with my Python package manager?
answer:
# uv Caching for Local Dependencies

**Caching Mechanism:**
For local dependencies, uv caches based on the last-modified time of the `pyproject.toml`, `setup.py`, or `setup.cfg` file. This means changes to your `setup.cfg` file will trigger a rebuild and reinstall.

**Options if Caching Causes Problems:**

1. **Clear the entire cache:** Run `uv cache clean`
2. **Clear cache for a specific package:** Run `uv cache clean <package-name>`
3. **Force rebuilds:** Add the package to `tool.uv.reinstall-package` list in your `pyproject.toml` to force rebuilds on every run
4. **Add custom cache keys:** Use `tool.uv.cache-keys` to incorporate additional file paths or Git commit hashes into the cache key for more granular control

# Docker with pnpm deploy

According to the context, Docker can be used with `pnpm deploy` to create portable deployments through a multi-stage build approach:

1. **First stage**: Build your entire monorepo
2. **Second stage**: Use `pnpm deploy` to extract only the necessary package and its dependencies:
   ```
   RUN pnpm --filter <your package name> --prod deploy pruned
   ```
3. **Final stage**: Copy the pruned deployment directory into a lightweight base image (e.g., `node:22-alpine`)

This approach creates a self-contained, portable package because `pnpm deploy` copies the package files and installs all dependencies (including workspace dependencies) in an isolated `node_modules` directory. The result can be copied to a server and executed without additional steps, significantly reducing image size compared to copying the entire monorepo.

question: How does pnpm create symlinked node_modules structure when foo@1.0.0 depend on bar, and what files get hard linked to the content-addressable store?

# pnpm's Symlinked node_modules Structure

When foo@1.0.0 depends on bar@1.0.0, pnpm follows this process:

**Hard Linking:** All package files (index.js, package.json, etc.) are hard linked to a content-addressable store. These are the only "real" files in node_modules.

**Symlinking:** After hard linking, symbolic links create the nested dependency structure. Bar is symlinked into foo@1.0.0/node_modules, allowing foo to access its dependency.

**Circular Link Prevention:** Parent packages are placed in the same node_modules folder as their dependencies, avoiding circular symlinks. So foo's dependencies aren't in foo/node_modules; instead, foo exists alongside its own dependencies.

This approach allows different projects to have different dependency versions of the same package while storing files only once.

question: How does dedupePeerDependents handle peer dependencies when packages are shared across multiple projects?
answer:
According to the context, `dedupePeerDependents` deduplicates packages with peer dependencies across different workspace projects when there are no conflicting peer dependencies.

When enabled (default: true), if multiple projects share the same package with identical peer dependencies, they will use a single instance of that package. However, if peer dependencies conflict—such as when different projects require different versions of a peer dependency—deduplication cannot occur.

For example, if webpack has esbuild as a peer dependency and only one project has esbuild installed, both projects can share the same webpack instance. But if two projects require different versions of a peer dependency (like react@16 vs react@17), webpack must be installed separately for each project to satisfy their conflicting requirements.

Type: Boolean

When enabled, peer dependency suffixes use version-only identifiers (name@version) instead of full dep paths, eliminating nested suffixes like (foo@1.0.0(bar@2.0.0)). This dramatically reduces the number of package instances in projects with many recursive peer dependencies.
This is different from dedupePeerDependents, which deduplicates packages that have the same peer dependencies across different workspace projects. dedupePeers simplifies the peer dependency suffix format itself.

this rule, though - packages with peer dependencies.

  - foo@1.0.0

foo-parent-2.

question: How do you configure the module-name for namespace packages that have multiple root modules, and what is the difference in how module-name is specified compared to regular modules?

# Configuring module-name for Multiple Root Modules

For namespace packages with multiple root modules, set `module-name` to a **list of names**:

```toml
[tool.uv.build-backend]
module-name = ["foo", "bar"]
```

## Key Differences from Regular Modules

**Regular modules:** `module-name` is a string (e.g., `"FOO"`)

**Multiple root modules:** `module-name` is a list (e.g., `["foo", "bar"]`)

**Single namespace module:** `module-name` can be dotted (e.g., `"foo.bar"`)

The context notes this structure is **not recommended**—using a workspace with multiple packages is preferred. However, it's supported by explicitly declaring each module name as a list. Alternatively, you can use `namespace = true` to avoid explicit declaration, though this disables safety checks.

a FOO module in the root directory, as in the project structure:

FOO
└── __init__.py

pyproject.toml[tool.uv.build-backend]
module-name = "FOO"
module-root = ""

Namespace packages
Namespace packages are intended for use-cases where multiple packages write modules into a shared
namespace.
Namespace package modules are identified by a . in the module-name. For example, to package the

pyproject.toml
src
└── foo
    └── bar
        └── __init__.py

pyproject.toml[tool.uv.build-backend]
module-name = "foo.bar"

module-name

The name of the module directory inside module-root.
The default module name is the package name with dots and dashes replaced by underscores.
Package names need to be valid Python identifiers, and the directory needs to contain a
__init__.py. An exception are stubs packages, whose name ends with -stubs, with the stem
being the module name, and which contain a __init__.pyi file.
For namespace packages with a single module, the path can be dotted, e.g., foo.bar or
foo-stubs.bar.
For namespace packages with multiple modules, the path can be a list, e.g.,
["foo", "bar"]. We recommend using a single module per package, splitting multiple
packages into a workspace.
Note that using this option runs the risk of creating two packages with different names but
the same module names.

In the second example, we have three roots (cloud.database, cloud.database_pro,
billing.modules.database_pro), so namespace = true is required.

Important
The __init__.py file is not included in foo, since it's the shared namespace module.

│   └── __init__.py
└── bar
    └── __init__.py

pyproject.toml[tool.uv.build-backend]

pyproject.toml[tool.uv.build-backend]

Using namespace = true disables safety checks.

Unlike a regular override, which rewrites every matching edge unconditionally, a convergence override rewrites a dependency edge only when its version satisfies the range that edge declares:
pnpm-workspace.yamloverrides:
  "form-data@": 4.0.6

With the above, a dependency that declares form-data: "^4.0.5" is pinned to 4.0.6, while one that declares ^3.0.0 keeps its own resolution. This lets compatible consumers converge on a single version — now and for any dependent added in the future — without forcing an incompatible version on the rest of the graph.
Rules:

The value must be an exact version. A range, a dist-tag, or a - removal fails with ERR_PNPM_INVALID_CONVERGENCE_OVERRIDE. A catalog: reference is allowed as long as the catalog entry resolves to an exact version.

Tip
For more details on the PubGrub algorithm, see Internals of the PubGrub
algorithm.

In addition to PubGrub's base algorithm, we also use a heuristic that backtracks and switches the
order of two packages if they have been conflicting too much.
Forking
Python resolvers historically didn't support backtracking, and even with backtracking, resolution
was usually limited to single environment, which one specific architecture, operating system, Python
version, and Python implementation. Some packages use contradictory requirements for different
environments, for example:
numpy>=2,<3 ; python_version >= "3.11"
numpy>=1.16,<2 ; python_version < "3.11"

Since Python only allows one version of each package, a naive resolver would error here.

The best way to avoid mistakes when working with multiple versions of a package is to keep your
queries into the dependency graph rooted in operations on the workspace root, workspace members, or
the requested script. These are the natural entry-points to the graph and can give coherent
responses for operations such as "install the workspace dev group", "install member1 and
member2[extra]", or "install this script's declared dependencies".
Another way to put this is that when possible you should avoid iterating over the resolution
object to find a node. Only access resolution like a map using ids that were provided by another
part of the metadata. For a workspace, the workspace root is workspace.id and package entry points
are listed in the members array.

This breaks the core
assumption incremental resolvers make that the set of versions for a package is static and would
require to always fetch the metadata for all possibly reachable version.
Prioritization
Prioritization is important for both performance and for better resolutions.
If we try many versions we have to later discard, resolution is slow, both because we have to read
metadata we didn't need and because we have to track a lot of (conflict) information for this
discarded subtree.
There are expectations about which solution uv should choose, even if the version constraints allow
multiple solutions.

If there are no lower bounds, the resolver can (and often will)
backtrack down to the oldest version of a package. This isn't only problematic because it's slow,
the old version of the package often fails to build, or the resolver can end up picking a version
that's old enough that it doesn't depend on the conflicting package, but also doesn't work with your
code.
Lower bounds are particularly critical when writing a library. It's important to declare the lowest
version for each dependency that your library works with, and to validate that the bounds are
correct — testing with
--resolution lowest or --resolution lowest-direct. Otherwise, a user may
receive an old, incompatible version of one of your library's dependencies and the library will fail
with an unexpected error.
